DecisionRank:
On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers

Yanran Wu Affiliation: Meta Affiliation: Purdue University    Dian Yu Affiliation: Meta    Chongyang Bai Affiliation: Meta    Jieyi Zhang Affiliation: Meta    Rui Liu Affiliation: Meta    Tianyi Chen Affiliation: Meta    Shike Mei Affiliation: Meta    Hang Cui Affiliation: Meta    Frank Shyu Affiliation: Meta    Sandeep Pandey Affiliation: Meta    Luke Simon Affiliation: Meta    Chunwei Liu Affiliation: Purdue University    Xi Liu Affiliation: Meta
Abstract

Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM’s ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student’s rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19–23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5×24.5\times faster on TREC DL and 16.7×16.7\times faster on BRIGHT.

††date: October 30, 2026††correspondence: dianyu@meta.com, cbai@meta.com, chunwei@purdue.edu

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in document reranking, particularly through listwise methods like RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023) that autoregressively generate candidate identifiers in descending order of relevance. However, this multi-step decoding incurs substantial inference latency. Decision models address this latency by directly predicting choices or scores without generating text, as illustrated by Jev (Almeida, 2026) and AnyJev (Zhang et al., 2026a). In document reranking, single-token methods such as FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024) follow the same principle: they sort first-token document-ID logits to obtain the ranking. Training these scores to capture the ranking preferences of capable generative teachers is therefore critical to effective single-token reranking.

Conventionally, ranking knowledge is transferred by training the student on static rankings generated offline by the teacher (Sun et al., 2023; Gangi Reddy et al., 2024; Schlatt et al., 2025) via learning-to-rank objectives. However, such fixed supervision cannot adapt to the student’s evolving predictions, leaving the teacher unable to provide feedback on the student’s current ranking decisions. While on-policy distillation (OPD) provides dynamic, state-aware feedback and has demonstrated notable success in autoregressive generation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024), effectively enabling it to complement offline ranking supervision in single-token rerankers remains challenging due to the structural mismatch between sequential feedback and single-pass scoring.

Specifically, standard token-level OPD relies on autoregressive rollouts to obtain conditional teacher feedback, whereas a single-token reranker represents the entire ranking through a static score vector in a single forward pass. Given this discrepancy, naive distillation strategies are insufficient: matching only the teacher’s first-token distribution captures initial preferences but leaves subsequent conditional choices unused, while training the student to generate full ranking sequences creates a mismatch with the first-token scores used at inference. This raises our core question: How can we distill the sequential ranking preferences of an autoregressive teacher into a student that ranks all candidates in a single forward pass?

To address this question, we propose DecisionRank, a decision reranking model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (Figure 2). Rather than relying on autoregressive student rollouts, we sort the student’s first-token scores to construct ranking prefixes from its current top-KK candidates. A frozen generative teacher evaluates these prefixes in a single teacher-forced forward pass, providing conditional choice distributions over the remaining candidates at each ranking step. We obtain the corresponding student distributions by normalizing its first-token scores over the same remaining candidates, and align them with the teacher distributions using reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence in item space. This directly supervises the student’s first-token scores used for inference, while allowing teacher feedback to adapt as the student’s ranking evolves. Because the alignment operates over candidate identities rather than vocabulary tokens, the teacher and student need not share a vocabulary or model architecture. We jointly optimize this on-policy objective with offline RankNet supervision derived from teacher-generated rankings, combining global ordering preferences with conditional feedback on the student’s current ranking. At inference, the student preserves its single-pass efficiency, ranking the full candidate set without autoregressive generation.

We conduct extensive experiments across four benchmarks covering both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks. Our method achieves a strong effectiveness–latency tradeoff compared with existing LLM-based rerankers. As shown in Figure 1, all three distilled students (1.7B, 4B, and 8B) outperform the 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19–23 (Craswell et al., 2020; Craswell et al., 2025). Notably, our 8B student also surpasses the listwise DirectRank-8B while running 24.5×24.5\times faster on TREC DL under the same input length settings. Our method consistently improves ranking effectiveness over offline RankNet supervision across all four benchmarks and outperforms alternative training objectives, including Offline KL, autoregressive SFT, autoregressive OPD, and Listwise GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Prabhakar et al., 2026). Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary benefits of offline RankNet supervision and on-policy distillation, with their combination achieving the strongest performance. Beyond ranking effectiveness, our 8B students yield lower pairwise calibration error than their Qwen3.8 and Gemma teachers on TREC DL and BRIGHT, without a calibration-specific training objective (Section 3.2.3).

The contributions of this paper are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce item-space on-policy distillation and combine it with offline ranking supervision to distill the ranking ability of generative LLM teachers into DecisionRank, a decision model for document reranking.

  • •

    We show that DecisionRank achieves competitive performance across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, with substantially lower inference latency than generative listwise rerankers.

  • •

    We demonstrate generalizability across teacher families and student sizes, with consistent improvements over zero-shot students across all 4 benchmarks.

2 Method

DecisionRank is a decision model for document reranking that learns from a generative teacher. It combines offline ranking supervision with on-policy feedback (Figure 2). In this section, we describe the 3 key components of our method. First-Token Ranking and Item-Space Alignment uses first-token document-ID logits as ranking scores and aligns teacher and student choice distributions over the same candidate items. On-Policy Conditional Feedback uses the student’s current ranking as a sequence of document selections. The teacher evaluates the remaining documents given those already selected, providing feedback to supervise the student’s scores. Offline Supervision and Joint Training combines this feedback with global ordering preferences from offline teacher rankings.

2.1 First-Token Ranking and Item-Space Alignment

Given a query qq and retrieved candidates D=(d1,…,dN)D=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{N}) with N≤100N\leq 100, the student reads the query and all candidates together. We assign each candidate did_{i} a distinct document ID viv_{i} from a pool of 100 single-token IDs in the student vocabulary. Let sis_{i} denote the logit of viv_{i} at the first output position. Sorting these scores yields the student’s ranking:

π=(π1,π2,…,πN)=argsorti∈{1,…,N}↓​si.\pi=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\ldots,\pi_{N})=\operatorname{argsort}_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}}^{\downarrow}s_{i}. (1)

Each candidate document did_{i} is an item in our ranking problem. The teacher uses numerical document IDs, while the student uses single-token IDs. Although these IDs can have different token representations, they refer to the same candidate items. We align the two models’ predictions for each item and compare their choice probabilities over the same candidate set. This item-space alignment enables distillation across model families.

2.2 On-Policy Conditional Feedback

To obtain on-policy feedback, we use the student’s current ranking to construct a sequence of selection decisions and query the teacher at the resulting states. We select the top-KK candidates S={π1,…,πK}S=\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{K}\} and follow their order in π\pi. At step tt, let ht=(π1,…,πt−1)h_{t}=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{t-1}) record the student’s earlier selections and Rt=S∖{π1,…,πt−1}R_{t}=S\setminus\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{t-1}\} contain the remaining candidates. The student’s scores define a Plackett–Luce choice distribution over RtR_{t}:

pθ,t​(i)=exp⁡(si)∑j∈Rtexp⁡(sj),i∈Rt.p_{\theta,t}(i)=\frac{\exp(s_{i})}{\sum_{j\in R_{t}}\exp(s_{j})},\qquad i\in R_{t}. (2)

Every step reuses the same first-token scores; only the remaining set changes. The trajectory itself is the deterministic ranking induced by those scores.

We construct the teacher prompt from qq and the selected documents DSD_{S}, retaining their first-stage retrieval order. We express the student’s ranking using the teacher’s numerical IDs and use it as the teacher-forced answer sequence. At step tt, the teacher evaluates the remaining items given the earlier student selections hth_{t}. Let aT,t​(i)>0a_{T,t}(i)>0 denote its conditional score for selecting item did_{i}. We map these scores to the corresponding candidate items and normalize over the remaining set RtR_{t}:

pT,t​(i)=aT,t​(i)∑j∈RtaT,t​(j),i∈Rt.p_{T,t}(i)=\frac{a_{T,t}(i)}{\sum_{j\in R_{t}}a_{T,t}(j)},\qquad i\in R_{t}. (3)

Both distributions are therefore defined over the same remaining items at every step. All conditional distributions are extracted in one teacher-forced forward pass over the student-induced answer sequence. This supplies feedback on the ranking states visited by the current student without an autoregressive rollout.

We align the student’s choices with the teacher’s conditional choices using reverse KL:

ℓt=DKL(pθ,t∥pT,t)=∑i∈Rtpθ,t(i)logpθ,t​(i)pT,t​(i).\ell_{t}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\theta,t}\,\|\,p_{T,t}\right)=\sum_{i\in R_{t}}p_{\theta,t}(i)\log\frac{p_{\theta,t}(i)}{p_{T,t}(i)}. (4)

The on-policy objective ℒon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{on}} averages these step divergences over a designated set of steps TstepT_{\mathrm{step}}:

ℒon=1|Tstep|​∑t∈Tstepℓt.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{on}}=\frac{1}{|T_{\mathrm{step}}|}\sum_{t\in T_{\mathrm{step}}}\ell_{t}. (5)

In joint training, we use Tstep={2,…,K−1}T_{\mathrm{step}}=\{2,\ldots,K-1\}. Starting from step 2 focuses the feedback on choices conditioned on earlier student selections, while offline supervision provides global ordering guidance. The final step is omitted because only one candidate remains and its KL divergence is zero.

Within each training step, the selected candidates and their order are fixed when computing the loss. Gradients update the student through its first-token scores, encouraging its choice distributions to agree with the teacher’s conditional preferences. As training updates these scores, we recompute the ranking and obtain teacher feedback on the student’s current selections.

2.3 Offline Supervision and Joint Training

The frozen teacher also provides full rankings generated offline using a sliding window with window size WW and stride ss. We supervise the student’s first-token scores on these static teacher rankings using RankNet (Burges et al., 2005):

ℒRN=∑(i,j)∈𝒫wi​j​log⁡(1+exp⁡(sj−si))∑(i,j)∈𝒫wi​j,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RN}}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}w_{ij}\log\left(1+\exp(s_{j}-s_{i})\right)}{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}w_{ij}}, (6)

where 𝒫={(i,j)∣di≻dj}\mathcal{P}=\{(i,j)\mid d_{i}\succ d_{j}\} contains pairs where did_{i} is ranked above djd_{j} by the teacher. Let riTr_{i}^{T} denote the teacher rank of did_{i}. We use the rank utility u⁡(r)=1/log2⁡(1+r)u(r)=1/\log_{2}(1+r) and weight each pair by wi​j=u⁡(riT)−u⁡(rjT)w_{ij}=u(r_{i}^{T})-u(r_{j}^{T}).

The complete training objective combines global ordering supervision with conditional feedback on the student’s current selections:

ℒ=ℒRN+λ​ℒon,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RN}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{on}}, (7)

where λ>0\lambda>0 controls the contribution of on-policy feedback. Offline RankNet supervises the global ordering across the full candidate set. On-policy distillation adds conditional feedback on the student’s current top-KK selections. Both objectives optimize the same first-token scores used at inference, while the teacher remains frozen throughout training.

Single-pass inference.

During inference, the trained student processes the query qq and the full candidate set of NN retrieved documents in a single forward pass, extracts their first-token identifier logits, and returns the ranking permutation π\pi via Equation 1. The full candidate ordering is obtained by sorting scores, with no autoregressive sequence generation.

3 Experiments

We organize our experiments around four research questions:

  1. RQ1.

    How does our method compare with existing rerankers?

  2. RQ2.

    Which training objective works best for ranking with first-token logits?

  3. RQ3.

    Does combining offline and on-policy supervision improve ranking?

  4. RQ4.

    Does our method generalize across teachers and student sizes?

3.1 Experimental Setup

3.1.1 Training

Training data.

We train on 10,000 MS MARCO queries from Rank-DistiLLM (Schlatt et al., 2025) and 6,000 synthetic queries from ReasonEmbed (Chen et al., 2026). For ReasonEmbed, we sample 500 queries from each of the 12 categories in the released dataset. For Rank-DistiLLM, we rerank the candidate documents with the corresponding teacher to construct offline ranking supervision.

Students and teachers.

Our students are initialized from Qwen3 at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters (Yang et al., 2025). Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) serves as the teacher for the main experiments. All teachers remain frozen and provide both offline rankings and on-policy feedback. To evaluate generalizability across teachers, we also distill from Gemma-4-31B (Gemma Team, 2026) and ReasonRank-32B (Liu et al., 2026) (Section 3.5). Training and inference details are provided in Appendix A.

3.1.2 Evaluation

Benchmarks and candidates.

We evaluate reranking effectiveness on 4 benchmarks spanning general and reasoning-intensive retrieval. \scriptsize1⃝ General retrieval benchmarks. We evaluate on the 5 TREC DL years from DL19 to DL23 (Craswell et al., 2020; Craswell et al., 2025), using the MS MARCO passage collections (Bajaj et al., 2018): DL19–20 use the v1 collection and DL21–23 use v2. To assess out-of-domain general retrieval, we evaluate on 7 BEIR datasets (Thakur et al., 2021): TREC-COVID, NFCorpus, DBPedia, SciFact, Signal-1M, TREC-News, and Robust04. Both TREC DL and BEIR use BM25 top-100 candidates. \scriptsize2⃝ Reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks. BRIGHT comprises 12 tasks spanning diverse domains (Su et al., 2025). We use top-100 candidates retrieved by ReasonIR-8B (Shao et al., 2025) with the released GPT-4 reasoning queries, while rerankers receive the original query. R2MED evaluates out-of-domain transfer to medical reasoning retrieval across 8 datasets (Zhang et al., 2026b), using top-100 candidates retrieved by E5-Mistral-7B-Instruct (Wang et al., 2024). Out-of-domain evaluation here refers to transfer beyond our distillation training data.

Evaluation metric.

We report normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (nDCG@10), which measures relevance among the top 10 results while assigning greater weight to higher ranks:

nDCG​@​10⁡(q,π)=1IDCG​@​10⁡(q)​∑r=110gq​(dπr)log2⁡(r+1).\operatorname{nDCG@10}(q,\pi)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{IDCG@10}(q)}\sum_{r=1}^{10}\frac{g_{q}(d_{\pi_{r}})}{\log_{2}(r+1)}. (8)

Here, π=(π1,…,πN)\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{N}) orders the NN candidate documents for query qq: πr\pi_{r} is the index of the document placed at rank rr, and dπrd_{\pi_{r}} is that document. The gain gq​(d)g_{q}(d) quantifies the relevance of document dd to query qq using the benchmark’s annotated relevance judgments (qrels). Irrelevant documents receive zero gain, and higher relevance grades receive larger gains, following the benchmark’s gain mapping. IDCG​@​10⁡(q)\operatorname{IDCG@10}(q) is the same discounted sum for the ideal ranking, computed from the benchmark’s full relevance judgments for qq. We first average over queries within each dataset, then take an unweighted mean over the 5 TREC DL years, 7 BEIR datasets, 12 BRIGHT tasks, or 8 R2MED datasets. All scores are multiplied by 100; higher is better.

3.2 RQ1: How does our method compare with existing rerankers?

We compare our method with pointwise and listwise rerankers. Pointwise methods score each query–document pair independently, while listwise methods consider multiple documents together. We evaluate ranking effectiveness across all 4 benchmarks, then examine inference efficiency and score calibration on TREC DL and BRIGHT.

3.2.1 Ranking Effectiveness

Table 1 compares our three student sizes with existing rerankers on general retrieval and reasoning-intensive retrieval. We also include Jev (Almeida, 2026) (jev-1.14.0) through its pointwise Score and listwise Choice interfaces. Score ranks documents by expected relevance grade, while Choice ranks all 100 candidates by their returned choice probabilities.

General retrieval.

All three student sizes outperform the compared baselines on both TREC DL and BEIR. Our 8B student improves over the strongest baseline, listwise DirectRank, by 1.42 points on TREC DL and 2.20 points on BEIR. The advantage already appears at 1.7B: our smallest student exceeds every compared baseline on both benchmark averages, including models with up to 32B parameters.

Reasoning-intensive retrieval.

Our 8B student achieves the highest average score on BRIGHT, and both 4B and 8B students outperform all open-weight pointwise baselines on BRIGHT and R2MED. The 8B student reaches 36.86 on BRIGHT, improving over listwise DirectRank by 0.99 points. On R2MED, it achieves 43.55, compared with 44.50 for listwise DirectRank. With just 16,000 training queries, our method distills the teacher’s ability to rerank reasoning-intensive queries and transfers this ability to out-of-domain medical retrieval.

3.2.2 Inference Efficiency

Figure 3 compares ranking effectiveness against single-query latency on TREC DL and BRIGHT to assess the efficiency of full-list reranking. Latency measurement details are provided in Appendix A.

Our three students form the effectiveness–latency Pareto frontier among locally evaluated models on both benchmarks. Even our 1.7B student achieves higher nDCG@10 and lower latency than Jev in both its pointwise and listwise modes on TREC DL. It also achieves the lowest latency on both benchmarks. On BRIGHT, our 4B student offers comparable ranking effectiveness and latency to Jev’s listwise mode. Our 8B student outperforms listwise DirectRank on both benchmarks while running 24.5×24.5\times faster on TREC DL and 16.7×16.7\times faster on BRIGHT.

3.2.3 Score Calibration

A ranker’s confidence is more useful if it reflects how often its preferences are correct. We compare DecisionRank with its generative teachers and the proprietary decision model Jev. We also include DirectRank-8B and ERank-32B, representing the two strongest open-weight pointwise reranker families by average ranking effectiveness in Table 1. We evaluate pairwise score calibration (Peng et al., 2023) using expected calibration error (ECE) (Guo et al., 2017). For pairs of documents with different relevance grades, each model assigns a probability to its predicted preference. We group these predictions into bins and measure the gap between average confidence and empirical accuracy:

ECE=∑b=1B|Bb|M​|acc⁡(Bb)−conf⁡(Bb)|,M=∑b=1B|Bb|.\operatorname{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{|B_{b}|}{M}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_{b})-\operatorname{conf}(B_{b})\right|,\qquad M=\sum_{b=1}^{B}|B_{b}|. (9)

Here, BbB_{b} contains the document pairs in bin bb, acc⁡(Bb)\operatorname{acc}(B_{b}) is the fraction of correct pairwise predictions, and conf⁡(Bb)\operatorname{conf}(B_{b}) is their mean predicted confidence. Lower ECE indicates closer agreement between confidence and accuracy.

As shown in Figure 4, both DecisionRank students achieve lower ECE than their teachers on TREC DL and BRIGHT, measured over document pairs across all evaluation queries. On BRIGHT, their ECE is comparable to that of the proprietary decision model Jev and lower than that of pointwise DirectRank and ERank. DecisionRank achieves this level of calibration through ranking supervision alone, without a dedicated calibration objective. Details of the probability calculations and ECE aggregation, along with additional results for 4B students, are provided in Appendix C.2.

3.3 RQ2: Which training objective works best for ranking with first-token logits?

Here, we ask which form of teacher supervision best improves the first-token reranking scores used at inference. We compare five additional objectives on top of a common RankNet loss: offline logit distillation (Offline KL), autoregressive supervised fine-tuning (AR SFT), autoregressive on-policy distillation (AR OPD), Listwise GRPO, and our item-space on-policy distillation (Item-space OPD).

RankNet.

RankNet is a classic pairwise learning-to-rank loss (Burges et al., 2005). Following FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024), we use a weighted RankNet objective (Equation 6) as the foundation for distillation. The following objectives each add a different form of supervision to this common foundation.

+ Offline KL.

Offline KL matches the student’s first-token distribution to a fixed teacher distribution. Before training, we run the teacher on the full candidate set and cache its first-position distribution over candidate IDs. We then minimize forward KL, DKL(pT∥pS)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{T}\|p_{S}), with both distributions normalized over all candidate IDs at temperature 1.

+ Autoregressive SFT (AR SFT).

AR SFT teaches the student to generate the teacher’s ranking as an autoregressive sequence. We apply teacher-forced cross-entropy to the ranking tokens, following the joint ranking and language-model supervision in FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024). When prompted to rank 100 candidates in a single response, LLMs produce incomplete or invalid rankings for most queries. We therefore only generate the first 20 candidate IDs from the teacher’s offline ranking and use them as the SFT target. The student learns to generate this ranking sequence while RankNet loss supervises the full candidate set on the first token logits.

+ Autoregressive OPD (AR OPD).

AR OPD applies distillation at each candidate-ID position in a student-generated ranking, following the GKD paradigm (Agarwal et al., 2024). The student first generates 20 distinct candidate rankings autoregressively. We provide the teacher with the query and the selected candidates, and append the student-generated ranking as a teacher-forced response. At each ID position, both models predict the next candidate conditioned on the same student-generated prefix. We minimize reverse KL, DKL(pS∥pT)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{S}\|p_{T}), between the student’s and teacher’s next-ID distributions at steps 1–19, with both distributions renormalized over the remaining IDs within the sampled set of 20.

+ Listwise GRPO.

Listwise GRPO optimizes student-sampled rankings with an nDCG@10 reward, aligning with the final evaluation metric. The teacher’s offline ranking provides the reference for computing this reward. We adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to ranking, drawing on the ranking-policy formulation of Prabhakar et al. (2026). The student’s first-token scores define a stochastic ranking policy: a probability distribution over candidate orderings. For a query qq and candidates D=(d1,…,dN)D=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{N}), let π=(π1,…,π|π|)\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{|\pi|}) denote a sampled ordering of distinct candidate indices, where πt\pi_{t} is the index selected at position tt and |π||\pi| is the ranking length. The policy assigns probability Pθ​(π∣q,D)P_{\theta}(\pi\mid q,D) to this ordering, where θ\theta denotes the student parameters. Using its first-token scores sis_{i}, we define this probability through the Plackett–Luce model:

Pθ​(π∣q,D)=∏t=1|π|exp⁡(sπt)∑j∈{1,…,N}∖{π1,…,πt−1}exp⁡(sj).P_{\theta}(\pi\mid q,D)=\prod_{t=1}^{|\pi|}\frac{\exp(s_{\pi_{t}})}{\sum_{j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{t-1}\}}\exp(s_{j})}. (10)

Each factor is the probability of selecting candidate πt\pi_{t} from those not yet selected; their product gives the probability of the sampled ordering. All selections reuse the same first-token scores from one student forward pass.

From this policy, we draw G=8G=8 rankings π(1),…,π(G)\pi^{(1)},\ldots,\pi^{(G)} per query using Gumbel sampling. If candidate ii has rank ρi\rho_{i} in the teacher’s offline ordering of NN candidates, we assign it relevance yi=(N−ρi)/(N−1)y_{i}=(N-\rho_{i})/(N-1), with gain 2yi−12^{y_{i}}-1. We compute an nDCG@10 reward for each sampled ranking and standardize the rewards within the group:

Rg=nDCG​@​10⁡(π(g);y),Ag=Rg−R¯σR,R_{g}=\operatorname{nDCG@10}(\pi^{(g)};y),\qquad A_{g}=\frac{R_{g}-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}}, (11)

where R¯\bar{R} and σR\sigma_{R} are the mean and standard deviation of the eight rewards. We update the student using these advantages, favoring rankings with above-average rewards. Rewards are computed from the same offline teacher ranking used by RankNet.

+ Item-space OPD (ours).

We design Item-space OPD to obtain corrective teacher feedback on the student’s ranking decisions. At each training step, the student’s first-token logits select and order its top-KK candidates. We provide these candidates to the teacher and use the student’s ranking as teacher-forced answer prefixes. A single forward pass yields the teacher’s conditional next-item distributions along these prefixes. We compute reverse KL in item space: teacher and student distributions are aligned by candidate IDs (Equation 4). This feedback guides the student’s ordering toward the teacher’s preferences. As the student’s ranking evolves, the teacher is queried on the updated candidates and prefixes. This type of loss directly applies to the first-token logits and is well-aligned with the student’s inference procedure.

Results.

As shown in Table 2, our method is the only method that consistently improves RankNet across all four benchmarks. Offline KL improves BRIGHT but degrades general retrieval and R2MED, suggesting that the teacher’s first-token distribution does not adequately capture ranking preferences beyond the initial selection. AR SFT and AR OPD improve reasoning-intensive retrieval but hurt general retrieval, consistent with a mismatch between sequence-generation training and first-token-score inference. Listwise GRPO provides ranking-level scalar rewards without explicit feedback on individual selections. In contrast, our method directly supervises the scores used at inference with conditional teacher feedback at each supervised selection step, achieving consistent gains across both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval.

3.4 RQ3: Does combining offline and on-policy supervision improve ranking?

Component ablation.

To answer this question, we compare RankNet alone, Item-space OPD alone, and their joint objective (Table 3). Zero-shot first-token scoring and sliding-window generation establish the student’s performance before distillation.

Results.

Joint training achieves the highest score among the student configurations on all four benchmarks. Adding Item-space OPD to RankNet improves both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval. The joint configuration also outperforms Item-space OPD alone across all four benchmarks, supporting the use of offline ranking supervision together with feedback on the student’s current predictions. These results show that the two forms of supervision are complementary: offline rankings provide a consistent training target, and on-policy feedback refines the first-token scores as the student’s ranking evolves.

Stability across training seeds.

The gains from on-policy feedback persist across training seeds. Table 4 compares RankNet and joint training for the 4B and 8B students on TREC DL and BRIGHT. Joint training improves over RankNet in every matched-seed comparison, covering both student sizes and both benchmarks. Appendix C.1 reports individual runs and paired significance tests.

3.5 RQ4: Does our method generalize across teachers and student sizes?

Our item-space alignment design enables students to learn from teachers across model families. To answer this question, we distill from Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B, and ReasonRank-32B into Qwen3 students at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters. ReasonRank-32B is built on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (Liu et al., 2026). Table 5 compares each student’s zero-shot performance with joint RankNet and Item-space OPD training under each teacher.

Results.

Our method generalizes across teacher families and student sizes, with consistent gains across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks. Each of the three teachers improves all three student sizes over their zero-shot counterparts on all four benchmarks.

4 Related Work

4.1 Efficient LLM-based Reranking

Generative listwise rerankers, such as RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023) and RankZephyr (Pradeep et al., 2023), produce rankings autoregressively, incurring decoding latency and repeated model calls for long candidate lists. TourRank (Chen et al., 2025a) and GroupRank (Long et al., 2026) improve efficiency through grouped comparisons and parallel processing. In contrast, FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024) eliminates ranking-sequence generation by sorting first-token document-ID logits, with subsequent work extending this approach (Chen et al., 2025b). Our work builds on first-token ranking and focuses on learning these scores from a generative teacher.

4.2 Knowledge Distillation for Reranking

Knowledge distillation transfers ranking knowledge from powerful teachers to smaller models. RankZephyr (Pradeep et al., 2023) and LiT5-Distill (Tamber et al., 2023) train generative rerankers on teacher-generated rankings, while Rank-DistiLLM (Schlatt et al., 2025) distills teacher rankings into cross-encoders using learning-to-rank objectives. DeAR (Abdallah et al., 2025) further incorporates reasoning-based supervision. Beyond offline distillation, GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024) and MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2024) leverage teacher feedback on student-generated sequences. Unlike these autoregressive approaches, DecisionRank applies on-policy teacher feedback directly to first-token ranking scores.

5 Conclusion

We introduced DecisionRank, a decision reranking model that combines offline ranking supervision with item-space on-policy distillation. Conditional teacher feedback on the student’s current ranking directly trains the first-token scores used at inference. This approach improves ranking across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval and generalizes across teacher families and student sizes. On TREC DL and BRIGHT, our 8B model outperforms its generative listwise counterpart with substantially lower latency. DecisionRank learns from a generative teacher’s sequential ranking decisions while reranking the full candidate set through single-token scoring, offering a promising path to distilling efficient decision models for broader applications.

Appendix A Training and Inference Details

Training.

We use a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} for the 1.7B student and 6×10−66\times 10^{-6} for the 4B and 8B students. The joint objective uses the student’s top-KK candidates with K=20K=20, supervises steps Tstep={2,…,19}T_{\mathrm{step}}=\{2,\ldots,19\}, and sets λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. Both losses update the student through its first-token scores. Candidate selection follows the student’s ranking without positive-document replacement. The OPD-only configuration in Section 3.4 uses loss weight 1 and supervises steps 1–19.

Teacher supervision.

All teacher–student combinations use the same training queries and first-token student inference. We obtain offline rankings and teacher reference scores using generative sliding windows of size W=20W=20 and stride s=10s=10, with thinking disabled for all teachers. The zero-shot student generation reference uses the same window size, stride, and thinking-disabled setting. On-policy feedback uses thinking-disabled configurations for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen3.8-27B, and a thinking-enabled configuration for ReasonRank-32B.

Inference.

At inference, the student scores the full candidate set in one forward pass. Student inputs truncate each passage to 128 tokens for TREC DL and 384 tokens for BEIR, BRIGHT, and R2MED. The main comparison evaluates baselines using the document budgets and inference parameters of their original implementations; Qwen3-Reranker uses the same passage-length limits as our students.

Jev API evaluation.

We use Jev (jev-1.14.0) through its Score and Choice interfaces. Score evaluates each query–document pair against 4 ordered relevance grades: 0 (irrelevant), 1 (related but does not answer the query), 2 (highly relevant), and 3 (perfectly relevant). Let pi​(r)p_{i}(r) denote the probability of grade rr for document did_{i}. We rank documents by the API’s returned expected relevance score,

siJev=∑r=03r​pi​(r).s_{i}^{\mathrm{Jev}}=\sum_{r=0}^{3}r\,p_{i}(r). (12)

Score questions are batched using the same passage-length limits as our students. Choice presents all 100 candidates as options in one question and ranks them by their returned probabilities. Passages are shortened uniformly when needed to fit the API context. Both modes break ties using retrieval order. To make the latency comparison fairer, we use server-reported time to exclude client-side network and connection delays. Queries are processed sequentially, and we report median per-query latency from the x-envoy-upstream-service-time response header, converted from milliseconds to seconds.

Latency measurement.

For the local models in Section 3.2.2, we use each method’s original inference configuration with passages truncated to 128 tokens for TREC DL and 384 tokens for BRIGHT, measuring both effectiveness and latency under these settings. We rerank 100 candidates from BM25 and ReasonIR-8B, respectively, using one vLLM worker per NVIDIA B200. After warm-up, queries are processed individually; we take the median latency per worker, then the median across 8 workers. Pointwise rerankers process all 100 query–document pairs concurrently; timing ends when all scores are available. Listwise timings include all required model calls and decoding steps. Student timings cover the forward pass and exclude score sorting.

Listwise ranking prompt.

System: You are RankLLM, an intelligent assistant that can rank passages based on their relevancy to the query User: I will provide you with 100 passages, each indicated by an alphabetical identifier []. Rank the passages based on their relevance to the search query: {query}. [AA] {passage 1} [AB] {passage 2} ... [ET] {passage 100} Search Query: {query} Rank the 100 passages above based on their relevance to the search query. ... The output format should be [] > [], e.g., [AB] > [AA], ... Assistant prefix: <think> </think> [

Appendix C Training Stability and Score Calibration

C.1 Results across Training Seeds

Table 10 reports individual runs for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with the Qwen3.8-27B teacher. Training data and evaluation settings are shared across seeds 42, 43, and 44. For paired significance tests, each query’s scores are averaged across the 3 seeds before comparing the methods.

C.2 Pairwise Score Calibration

Pairwise predictions and confidence.

We evaluate pairs of candidate documents from the same query whose annotated relevance grades differ, treating unjudged documents as grade 0. Let gig_{i} denote the relevance grade of did_{i}, and let ui​ju_{ij} be the probability that the model assigns to preferring did_{i} over djd_{j}. Values above 1/21/2 favor did_{i}, while values below 1/21/2 favor djd_{j}. We record whether the predicted preference agrees with the relevance judgments:

yi​j=[(ui​j>1/2)=(gi>gj)].y_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[(u_{ij}>1/2)=(g_{i}>g_{j})\right]. (13)

Its confidence ci​jc_{ij} is the probability assigned to the preferred document. We express the strength of this preference through the absolute log-odds δi​j\delta_{ij}:

δi​j=|log⁡ui​j1−ui​j|,ci​j=max⁡(ui​j,1−ui​j)=σ⁡(δi​j),\delta_{ij}=\left|\log\frac{u_{ij}}{1-u_{ij}}\right|,\qquad c_{ij}=\max(u_{ij},1-u_{ij})=\sigma(\delta_{ij}), (14)

where σ⁡(x)=1/(1+exp⁡(−x))\sigma(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x)) is the sigmoid function. A gap of δi​j=0\delta_{ij}=0 corresponds to confidence 1/21/2; larger gaps indicate stronger preferences. Calibration measures how closely these confidence values match the frequency of correct predictions. We obtain ui​ju_{ij} from each model as follows.

DecisionRank students.

The student assigns each document a first-token document-ID logit sis_{i}. We convert the difference between two logits into a pairwise preference probability, as in the RankNet objective:

ui​j=σ⁡(si−sj),δi​j=|si−sj|,ci​j=σ⁡(|si−sj|).u_{ij}=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j}),\qquad\delta_{ij}=|s_{i}-s_{j}|,\qquad c_{ij}=\sigma(|s_{i}-s_{j}|). (15)

Thus, the student’s confidence is determined by how far apart its two ranking scores are.

Generative teachers.

For Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B, let pip_{i} denote the probability assigned to document ID ii at the first output position after reading all candidates. We normalize the two documents’ probabilities to obtain their pairwise preference:

ui​j=pipi+pj=σ⁡(log⁡pi−log⁡pj),ci​j=max⁡(pi,pj)pi+pj.u_{ij}=\frac{p_{i}}{p_{i}+p_{j}}=\sigma(\log p_{i}-\log p_{j}),\qquad c_{ij}=\frac{\max(p_{i},p_{j})}{p_{i}+p_{j}}. (16)

Here, δi​j=|log⁡pi−log⁡pj|\delta_{ij}=|\log p_{i}-\log p_{j}|. These probabilities measure the teacher’s preference between the two documents at its initial selection.

Pointwise rerankers.

DirectRank and ERank score each query–document pair separately. Let ziz_{i} denote the relevance score for document did_{i}. For DirectRank, this score is the log-odds of the relevance labels true and false:

zi=log⁡P⁡(true∣q,di)P⁡(false∣q,di).z_{i}=\log\frac{P(\mathrm{true}\mid q,d_{i})}{P(\mathrm{false}\mid q,d_{i})}. (17)

For ERank, ziz_{i} is its predicted document relevance score. Both models use the same conversion from score differences to pairwise probabilities and confidence:

ui​j=σ⁡(zi−zj),δi​j=|zi−zj|,ci​j=σ⁡(|zi−zj|).u_{ij}=\sigma(z_{i}-z_{j}),\qquad\delta_{ij}=|z_{i}-z_{j}|,\qquad c_{ij}=\sigma(|z_{i}-z_{j}|). (18)

A larger score difference produces a more confident pairwise preference. Both pointwise baselines in Figure 4 use this readout and the same binning and ECE calculation described below.

Jev.

Jev’s Score interface returns a distribution pi​(a)p_{i}(a) over 4 relevance grades, a∈{0,1,2,3}a\in\{0,1,2,3\}, for each document (Appendix A). Treating the predicted grades as independent, we form their joint distribution as pi​(a)​pj​(b)p_{i}(a)p_{j}(b) and compute

ui​j=∑a>bpi​(a)​pj​(b)+12​∑api​(a)​pj​(a).u_{ij}=\sum_{a>b}p_{i}(a)p_{j}(b)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a}p_{i}(a)p_{j}(a). (19)

The first term sums the probability of did_{i} receiving a higher grade than djd_{j}. The second splits the probability of equal predicted grades evenly between the two preferences. We then compute δi​j\delta_{ij} and ci​j=max⁡(ui​j,1−ui​j)c_{ij}=\max(u_{ij},1-u_{ij}) using Equation 14. Jev’s pairwise confidence therefore uses its full grade distributions. Its ranking scores use the expected grade in Equation 12.

Binning and ECE.

We examine calibration as a function of the score gap, following Peng et al. (2023). We group pairs by δi​j\delta_{ij} into bins [0,0.5),[0.5,1),…,[7.5,8)[0,0.5),[0.5,1),\ldots,[7.5,8) and [8,∞)[8,\infty). For each nonempty bin BbB_{b}, we compute mean confidence and empirical accuracy:

conf⁡(Bb)=1|Bb|​∑(i,j)∈Bbci​j,acc⁡(Bb)=1|Bb|​∑(i,j)∈Bbyi​j.\operatorname{conf}(B_{b})=\frac{1}{|B_{b}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in B_{b}}c_{ij},\qquad\operatorname{acc}(B_{b})=\frac{1}{|B_{b}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in B_{b}}y_{ij}. (20)

ECE is the absolute difference between these quantities, averaged over bins with weights proportional to their pair counts (Equation 9). We pool valid pairs across all queries within each benchmark, so queries with more eligible pairs contribute more weight. Overall pairwise accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions across these pairs. Each model uses the valid pairs available in its recorded outputs; all models use the same evaluation queries and relevance judgments.

Full-benchmark score calibration.

Figures 5–8 use all evaluation queries and the original model scores. They compare the Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B teachers with their respective 8B and 4B students. The score-gap plots use |Δ|=δi​j|\Delta|=\delta_{ij} on the horizontal axis, with Δ=si−sj\Delta=s_{i}-s_{j} for students and Δ=log⁡pi−log⁡pj\Delta=\log p_{i}-\log p_{j} for teachers. Finite score-gap bins are plotted at their midpoints, with the δ≥8\delta\geq 8 bin shown separately. Both student sizes have lower ECE and higher pairwise accuracy than their respective teachers on TREC DL and BRIGHT.

Calibration of 4B students.

The same pattern extends to Qwen3-4B: under both teachers, the student achieves lower aggregate ECE and higher overall pairwise accuracy on TREC DL and BRIGHT. Figures 7 and 8 use the same binning, axis ranges, and visual layout as the 8B plots, enabling direct comparison across student sizes.

Results.

The calibration gains are consistent across teacher families and student sizes. On TREC DL and BRIGHT, the 4B and 8B DecisionRank students trained with either Qwen3.8-27B or Gemma-4-31B achieve lower ECE and higher pairwise accuracy than their corresponding teachers. DecisionRank achieves this improved calibration through ranking supervision alone, without a dedicated calibration objective.
